items.title: Dipole moment and polarity of molecules

source_refs.note: The unnumbered topic Dipole Moment and Polarity of Molecules, printed pages 51-52 (Figures 3.5 to 3.7), with Quick Check 3.4 as the self-check.

blocks.text: In compounds such as HF, where the bonded atoms are of different elements, the electron distribution between the atoms is uneven, so one atom carries a partial positive charge and the other a partial negative charge. A molecule with a delta+ charge on one part and a delta- charge on the other is a dipole, and such a molecule is said to have a dipole moment. The dipole moment is a quantitative measure of the polarity of a bond or a molecule. The dipole moments of diatomic molecules such as HF, HCl, HBr, HI and NO are directed from the positive end (delta+) to the negative end (delta-); in HF the electron density is higher near the fluorine atom and the moment points from H to F. Dipole moment is measured in the debye unit (D); a higher dipole moment means higher polarity.

blocks.alt: Left: a dot picture of the electron cloud of HF, thicker around the fluorine nucleus than the hydrogen nucleus. Right: H (delta+) bonded to a larger F (delta-), with a crossed arrow drawn from the H end to the F end showing the dipole.
blocks.caption: Electron density in HF is higher near F; the dipole moment points from H to F (original diagram after Figure 3.5).

blocks.text: For compounds with more than two atoms the dipole moment depends on the structure of the molecule. The dipole moment of water is 1.85 D, directed from the end with the two hydrogen atoms to the end with the oxygen atom. A linear H-O-H molecule would have zero dipole moment, so the non-zero value shows that water is non-linear; experiments reveal a v-shaped structure. SO2 has a dipole moment of 1.61 D in the opposite direction to that in water. H2S is also non-linear: its bonds are polar and do not cancel, so the molecule has a dipole moment.

blocks.alt: Left: a bent H2O molecule with delta- on O and delta+ on each H; bond-moment arrows point from H to O and the resultant points up to O; P = 1.85 D. Right: a bent SO2 molecule with delta+ on S and delta- on each O; the bond-moment arrows point from S to O and the resultant points down, away from S; P = 1.61 D. Below: a coloured electron density map of water, red at the oxygen end and blue at the hydrogen end, with the printed note that the dipole moment is from blue to red.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.6: Vector addition of individual bond moments in angular H2O and SO2 molecules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.6).

blocks.text: Some molecules have zero dipole moment because the symmetry of their structure cancels the individual bond moments. BeCl2 is linear with two similar chlorine atoms on either side of the central atom at 180 degrees, so the Be-Cl bond moments, equal and opposite, cancel. CCl4 has four C-Cl bonds expected to be highly polar from the large electronegativity difference between C and Cl, but the four bond moments are directed so that they cancel; the net dipole moment is zero and the molecule is non-polar and perfectly tetrahedral. BF3 has a symmetrical trigonal planar structure and its dipole moment is also zero. As a rule, in molecules with the same ligands (atoms or groups attached to the central atom) in a regular geometry the individual bond moments may not be zero, but the overall molecule has zero dipole moment and is non-polar.

blocks.alt: Three symmetrical molecules, each with p = 0 D beneath it. BeCl2 is linear, Cl-Be-Cl, with a 180 degree arc. BF3 is trigonal with delta+ on B, delta- on each F and a bond-moment arrow beside each B-F bond pointing to F. CCl4 is drawn as a tetrahedral sketch with delta+ on C, delta- on each Cl and a bond-moment arrow beside each C-Cl bond pointing to Cl. The moments cancel.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.7: The individual bond moments in symmetrical molecules BeCl2, BF3 and CCl4 cancel out to give zero net dipole moment (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.7; the printed caption says CH4).
